line: Your pocket aces don't always get cracked. You just keep letting five people try.
open_question: Why do pocket aces seem to lose so often?

line: Against one player who stays to the river, pocket aces win 85% of the time. Against five, 49%. Count the chairs before you blame the deck.
open_question: What changes between the aces that hold and the aces that lose?

line: Nobody at your table ever folds, and you still wonder why your pocket aces keep losing.
open_question: What does a table that never folds do to pocket aces?

line: Slow-play pocket aces to set a trap and you can let five players in. Against five who stay to the river, aces win only 49% of the time.
open_question: What does letting players in cheaply cost pocket aces?

line: Before you call the app rigged because your aces lost again, count how many players stayed in the hand.
open_question: If it isn't rigged, why do aces lose so much on the app?

line: You look down at pocket aces and your stomach drops, because you think you know how this ends. The reason isn't bad luck.
open_question: What is the reason aces keep ending badly, if not luck?

line: Some players feel safer holding suited connectors than pocket aces. The aces aren't the problem. The crowd in the pot is.
open_question: Why do pocket aces feel worse to play than they should?

line: Somebody at every table jokes that they just fold pocket aces now. The fix is smaller than that: fewer players in the pot.
open_question: How much do fewer players in the pot change what aces win?

line: Pocket aces lose to one player who stays to the river about 15% of the time. So why does it feel like yours lose every time?
open_question: Why do your aces lose far more often than they do against one player?

line: Pocket aces against one player who stays to the river: 85%. Against two: 73%. Three: 64%. Four: 56%. Five: 49%. That last one is your home game.
open_question: How much does each extra player take from pocket aces?

line: The home game where everybody sees every flop is the same home game where everybody swears pocket aces are cursed.
open_question: What do those two things have to do with each other?

line: You know the player who calls every bet with any two cards. Put five of him in a pot to the river and your pocket aces win 49% of the time.
open_question: What do players who call everything do to pocket aces?

line: You raised your pocket aces and four players called anyway. If all four stay to the river, your aces win 56% of the time.
open_question: Where did the rest of the aces' edge go?

line: You can lose with pocket aces and shrug. It gets easier once you start counting how many players were in the pot.
open_question: Why does counting the players make a cracked pair of aces easier to take?

line: "My aces always get cracked." Next time you say it, finish the sentence: against how many players?
open_question: How much does the number of players decide whether aces hold?

line: Twenty all-ins before the flop with pocket aces, one player each time: a 96% chance you lose at least one. Now picture five players.
open_question: If aces lose sometimes even against one player, what happens against a crowd?

line: Five players who stay to the river turn pocket aces into a hand that wins 49% of the time. You didn't get unlucky. You got company.
open_question: Why is it the company, not luck, that beats pocket aces?

line: Every player who called your pocket aces had a worse hand than you. Five of them together, if they stay to the river, win about as often as you do.
open_question: How do five worse hands add up to beat the best one?

line: Pocket aces are one pair. A very good pair, and still just one pair against every player you let see the river.
open_question: How much weaker does that one pair get with each player who sees the river?

line: Stop blaming the river card for your pocket aces. Blame how many players were still there to see it.
open_question: Why does the number of players at the river matter more than the card?
